title: The Line of the Pasaje: the Gaucho War, the Debased Coin, and the Ten Days at the Horqueta
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Salta, the Colegio, and the Two Invasions

stops.name: Salta, the birth under the Cerro San Bernardo
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the city of Salta, in the northwest of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata, a son is born on the eighth of February to a family of the local governing class. The house itself has never been identified, so the cathedral square stands for the whole town: a grid of adobe under the Cerro San Bernardo, four hundred leagues from Buenos Aires and a few days' ride from the Andean passes that carry silver down from Potosí. The frontier he will spend his life holding begins at the end of his own street, and the road to the capital that will disown him begins at the other end.
suggested_refs: The cathedral square of Salta, standing in for an unidentified birth house

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Real Colegio de San Carlos
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the college's own record does not name him, and the year is approximate
stops.campa: The boy is sent down to Buenos Aires and put into the Real Colegio de San Carlos, in the block of buildings later called the Manzana de las Luces, with private instruction in philosophy and the sciences alongside the college's curriculum. The college's own record, as it reaches the present, does not name him among its students; the schooling rests on his biographers rather than on a register. He learns the capital in the same years he learns Latin. It is the same city whose government will annul his currency in 1818.
suggested_refs: The Manzana de las Luces and the Real Colegio de San Carlos, Buenos Aires
sources: Wikipedia, 'Real Colegio de San Carlos' (silent on Güemes, gap flagged)

stops.name: Salta, the Regimiento Fijo at fourteen
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month not established
stops.campa: At fourteen he enlists in the Regimiento Fijo de Infantería and is posted on detachment duty back to Salta, a cadet in his own town. He will wear a uniform for the rest of his life. In 1805, with the coast alarmed by the prospect of an English squadron, the regiment is called down to the capital and Güemes rides the long road south with it. He is twenty years old and has been a soldier for six of them. The war of ambush he becomes known for is learned first inside a line regiment, under orders.
suggested_refs: The Regimiento Fijo de Infantería and its Salta detachment

stops.name: The river shallows, the boarding of the Justine
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the episode descends through Cornejo and Frías, not through a contemporary document
stops.campa: During the reconquest of Buenos Aires from Beresford's occupation, the armed British merchantman Justine goes aground in the shallows of the Río de la Plata on a sudden fall of the river. Güemes leads a cavalry charge into the water and takes her from horseback. No contemporary document records the action: the story comes down through the biographers Atilio Cornejo and Bernardo Frías, and the ship was stranded on a mudbank rather than moored at a quay. The legend of the gaucho who captured a ship on a horse starts here.
suggested_refs: Atilio Cornejo, Historia de Güemes (1971), p. 46, the traditional source for the Justine

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the second invasion and the father's death
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Whitelocke's columns march into the city in July and are shot to pieces from the flat roofs by townspeople who were not an army the week before. Güemes fights in the defense, falls ill afterward, and in November his father dies. He is twenty-two, sick in a city that is not his, and now the head of a Salta household four hundred leagues away. What he has seen from the rooftops is townspeople breaking a professional army with no line of battle and no general anywhere in sight.
suggested_refs: The 1807 defense of Buenos Aires against Whitelocke

stops.name: Salta, the transfer home
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: His transfer back to Salta is approved on the tenth of March; by December he is carried on the rolls there as a lieutenant of the Cuerpo de Granaderos. Two years later the Cabildo of Buenos Aires deposes the viceroy and the northwest stops being a back province and becomes a war frontier. Güemes is already in place, known at every ranch and post-house between the Valle de Lerma and the Quebrada, and holding the rank that will put him at the head of a column when the first army goes north.
suggested_refs: The Cuerpo de Granaderos rolls at Salta, December 1808

stops.name: Quebrada de Humahuaca, the vanguard going north
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month approximate
stops.campa: The first auxiliary expedition to Upper Peru climbs the Quebrada de Humahuaca, a gorge of red and ochre rock that narrows the road to single file for a hundred and fifty kilometres. Güemes commands its vanguard. The column is under Colonel Francisco Ortiz de Ocampo, with Antonio González Balcarce second and Juan José Castelli as the Junta's political representative; Manuel Belgrano is at this moment leading the Paraguay campaign and will not take the Army of the North until March 1812. Güemes learns the gorge on this march and then holds it for eleven years.
suggested_refs: The Quebrada de Humahuaca, the single road between Jujuy and Upper Peru
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Primera expedición auxiliadora al Alto Perú'

stops.name: Suipacha, the charge that decides it
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the seventh of November, in the broken ground of Sud Chichas some twenty-five kilometres from Tupiza, the patriot force under González Balcarce breaks the royalists in the first outright victory of the revolution. Güemes, a captain, takes a decisive part in it with cavalry. Two days later Castelli sends him with a hundred and fifty mounted tarijeños to secure the head of Cinti and run down the fleeing royalist officials. He spends the following year in the valleys of Tarija, learning a kind of war that has no line of battle in it at all.
suggested_refs: The field of Suipacha in Sud Chichas, Potosí, first patriot victory of the revolution

stops.name: Huaqui, covering the retreat
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: At Huaqui, on the southeastern shore of Lake Titicaca, Goyeneche destroys the patriot army in a single morning, and the whole northern gain of the revolution is lost inside a week. Güemes is not in the rout. He is behind it, covering the withdrawal south with mounted parties and closing the passes as the army falls back through them. This is where the war of resources begins: the harrying of an enemy's mules, cattle and couriers instead of his order of battle. He will fight it without interruption for the next ten years.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Huaqui on Lake Titicaca, June 1811

stops.name: Tarija, recovered with the royalist booty
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of January, acting on orders from Juan Martín de Pueyrredón, Güemes recovers Tarija and rejoins the army with three hundred men, five hundred rifles and two cannon taken from the royalists. The figures are the spoils, not the force he brought: a partisan's arithmetic, in which what the enemy loses is what you gain. Royalist pressure under Goyeneche will push him back down to Jujuy before the year is out. By now the method is fixed, and it does not require holding any ground at all.
suggested_refs: Tarija and its valleys, retaken 18 January 1812 on Pueyrredón's orders

stops.name: Buenos Aires, removed to the General Staff
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the month is not established, and the order postdates Belgrano's assumption of command on 26 March 1812, so this date is nominal
stops.campa: Belgrano, who takes command of the Army of the North on the twenty-sixth of March, orders Güemes transferred to Buenos Aires and folded into the Estado Mayor General. The order removes him from the northern theatre altogether. He passes the next two years in the capital that schooled him, at a desk, while Belgrano conducts the Éxodo Jujeño and burns the province behind him. The gaucho parties of the Valle de Lerma go on operating without their captain, and they are still riding the same country when he comes back.
suggested_refs: The Estado Mayor General at Buenos Aires, 1812

segments.name: The Vanguard and the Valle de Lerma

stops.name: Campo de Castañares, the Battle of Salta
stops.date_confidence: the battle is attested; Güemes's presence is contradicted between sources and is not resolved here
stops.campa: On the field of Castañares north of the city, in rain, Belgrano defeats Pío Tristán and takes the surrender of a royalist army on its own ground. Salta's biographical tradition puts Güemes's gaucho cavalry on that field, sealing the retreat. The record of the battle itself names Belgrano and Eustoquio Díaz Vélez and does not name Güemes, and he is by this date attached to the General Staff in Buenos Aires. The sources contradict each other and are left contradicting. Salta is patriot ground again, and the man who will hold it is somewhere else.
suggested_refs: The Campo de Castañares north of Salta, 20 February 1813
sources: Wikipedia, 'Martín Miguel de Güemes' (places him there); contradiction flagged

stops.name: Posta de Yatasto, the army changes hands
stops.date_confidence: attested, but the atlas files disagree: san_martin.journey.json dates the meeting 17 January and belgrano.journey.json the handover 30 January 1814
stops.campa: At a post-house on the Salta road, in country Güemes knows better than either of them, Manuel Belgrano hands the beaten Army of the North to José de San Martín. San Martín's journey dates the meeting to the seventeenth of January and the handover to the twenty-ninth; Belgrano's dates it to the thirtieth. The two files disagree and are not reconciled here. What follows is not in dispute. San Martín looks at the northern passes, concludes that the road to Lima does not run through Upper Peru, and starts looking for a man to hold the door while he goes another way.
suggested_refs: The Posta de Yatasto on the Salta road, where the Army of the North changed commanders
sources: belgrano.journey.json (la entrega del ejército a San Martín)

stops.name: La Ciudadela, Tucumán, the frontier delegated
stops.date_confidence: attested per san_martin.journey.json
stops.campa: From the fortified camp of La Ciudadela outside Tucumán, San Martín rebuilds the army and gives the northern mountain frontier to Güemes and his gauchos to hold. He promotes him lieutenant colonel and puts him at the head of the vanguard. The arrangement suits both men exactly. San Martín is freed to open the western Andes and Chile; Güemes is given, in writing and by the highest authority in the field, the war he has been fighting without authorization since Huaqui. From this day he holds the north under a written commission from his commanding general.
suggested_refs: The camp of La Ciudadela outside San Miguel de Tucumán, January 1814

stops.name: Valle de Lerma, the gaucho war opens
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month approximate and the valley is a region, not a point
stops.campa: In the wide grass valley south of Salta, Güemes takes the mounted militia parties already operating there and turns them into a standing instrument. They are ranch hands, muleteers and peons who ride their own horses, carry lance and knife, know every ford and every dry gully, and go home to work between actions. The line they screen runs more than seven hundred kilometres, from Volcán in Jujuy to beyond San Ramón de la Nueva Orán. It resembles no European front in any particular. For seven years nothing gets through it.
suggested_refs: The Valle de Lerma south of Salta, cradle of the Guerra Gaucha

stops.name: Salta, María Remedios del Valle rides in
stops.date_confidence: attested per maria_remedios_del_valle.journey.json; month approximate
stops.campa: María Remedios del Valle, whom Belgrano's army called the Mother of the Homeland and whom the royalists flogged for nine days after Ayohuma, comes into the frontier war Güemes is building out of Salta's gauchos. She fights the ambush-and-retreat war of the Upper Peru border for the next seven years, part of that time under Arenales across the Salta and Tarija country. Her service certificate of 1827, signed in Buenos Aires by Colonel Hipólito Videla, names Güemes among her commanders. The certificate is sworn military testimony.
suggested_refs: The 1827 service certification of María Remedios del Valle, signed by Colonel Hipólito Videla
sources: maria_remedios_del_valle.journey.json (Salta, joining Güemes' gauchos; certification stop, 17 January 1827)

stops.name: Puesto del Marqués, the puna of Jujuy
stops.date_confidence: attested; the site lies near Abra Pampa in Jujuy and the coordinate is approximate
stops.campa: High on the puna, in Rondeau's third expedition to Upper Peru, patriot forces under Francisco Fernández de la Cruz, Martín Rodríguez and Güemes beat Antonio Vigil at Puesto del Marqués. The action belongs to Jujuy province and to 1815, not to Salta and not to 1814: two errors that have travelled together through the popular chronologies for a century. Afterward Güemes quarrels with Rondeau over supply and command and pulls his forces back into the high puna and northern Salta, trading ground for time, as he will keep on doing.
suggested_refs: Puesto del Marqués on the Jujuy puna, near Abra Pampa
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Combate de Puesto del Marqués'

stops.name: Salta, elected governor intendente
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the sixth of May the Cabildo of Salta elects Güemes governor intendente of a province that then takes in Jujuy, Tarija and Orán. He is the first governor of Salta raised by local authorities instead of appointed from Buenos Aires, and the gaucho militias standing outside the building are the reason. The capital will spend the next six years trying to work out whether he is a general of the republic or a caudillo who happens to be pointing his lances at the Spanish. He is both at once, and the question is never settled in his lifetime.
suggested_refs: The Cabildo of Salta, seat of the first locally elected governorship of the province

stops.name: Catedral de Salta, the marriage to Carmen Puch
stops.date_confidence: attested from his biography; the cathedral's own record does not mention the wedding
stops.campa: He marries Carmen Puch in the cathedral of Salta on the fifteenth of July, ten weeks into his governorship. She is from a landed Salta family; her beauty is the one thing every nineteenth-century account of her agrees on, and very little else about her is recorded anywhere. The cathedral's own history says nothing of the wedding, so the date comes from his biography rather than from the building's register. The same cathedral holds his bones now, and hers beside them, though the dates of the transfers are nowhere established.
suggested_refs: The Catedral de Salta, site of the 1815 marriage and of the later Panteón de las Glorias del Norte
sources: Wikipedia, 'Catedral de Salta' (silent on the wedding, gap flagged)

stops.name: Salta, the División Infernal de Gauchos de Línea
stops.date_confidence: the date is given by the secondary source that carries the quotation; the primary communication was not located
stops.campa: He reports to the Supreme Director that he has formed a cavalry division of two squadrons under the name División Infernal de Gauchos de Línea. The Infernales exist beyond any doubt; their red poncho and their name pass into Argentine memory and, a century and a half later, onto the uniform of the 5th Cavalry Regiment. The wording of the communication of the twelfth of September has not been traced to an archival edition, so the sentence below stands as attribution rather than as a document. What it names is not in question.
stops.quote: He organizado una división de caballería compuesta de dos escuadrones... con la denominación de División Infernal de Gauchos de Línea.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Güemes, official communication to the Supreme Director, 12 September 1815, cited in a secondary account of the Guerra Gaucha; primary document not located [R]
suggested_refs: The Infernales de Güemes and the red poncho later worn by the 5th Cavalry Regiment
sources: Secondary account of the Guerra Gaucha, quoted attribution [R]

stops.name: Cerrillos, the pact with Rondeau
stops.date_confidence: conventionally 22 March 1816; the popular chronologies date the pact to 1815, six months early, which the January 1816 siege makes impossible
stops.campa: Rondeau brings the Army of the North down on Salta in January 1816 and puts the city under siege, patriot against patriot. After some weeks of standoff the two men sign the Pacto de los Cerrillos. Güemes is recognized as governor and charged with the defense of the northern frontier; Rondeau gets his rear secured and marches away. Güemes gets on paper what his gauchos had already taken in fact: the republic writes down, in a treaty with one of its own generals, that the north is his to hold.
suggested_refs: The Pacto de los Cerrillos, signed at Cerrillos in the Valle de Lerma

stops.name: San Miguel de Tucumán, independence declared
stops.date_confidence: the declaration is attested; Güemes is not recorded as present
stops.campa: In a rented house in Tucumán the congress declares the United Provinces of South America independent of Ferdinand VII and of every other foreign domination. Güemes is not in the hall and is not recorded as having been anywhere near it. The claim made for him, in Salta first and afterward in the national canon, is that the congress could meet at all because his gauchos stood between it and the royalist army in the north. It is a claim about a thing that did not happen, and it cannot be proved. It is also the claim that carried him into the national canon.
suggested_refs: The Casa de la Independencia at San Miguel de Tucumán

stops.name: Tucumán, Belgrano's letter of the third of August
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Belgrano, restored to the command of the Army of the North at La Ciudadela, writes to Güemes about the congress's answer to his request for help and endorses the whole method of the gaucho war in a single sentence. The letter opens as one countryman to another. For the next three years the two men correspond: Belgrano holding the inner line at Tucumán and forwarding what supplies he can, Güemes fighting the actual frontier seven hundred kilometres wide. Neither one ever holds command over the other.
stops.quote: El pensamiento de Ud. es excelente; conviene animar la moral del soldado con pequeñas victorias y creo que tal vez pueda tener Ud. una que le llene de gloria y no menos restituya el concepto a nuestras armas que por desgracia está muy abatido.
stops.quote_source: Manuel Belgrano, letter to Güemes, 3 August 1816, quoted in the Spanish Wikipedia article on Güemes
suggested_refs: The Belgrano-Güemes correspondence, 1816-1819
sources: belgrano.journey.json (second command of the Army of the North)

stops.name: Volcán, Jujuy, the northern anchor of the line
stops.date_confidence: the line is held 1815-1821; this date is nominal and no personal action of Güemes is documented at this spot
stops.campa: At Volcán, where the Río Grande breaks out of the Quebrada de Humahuaca onto the floor of the Jujuy valley, the northern end of the frontier is anchored. From here the line runs south and east more than seven hundred kilometres to beyond San Ramón de la Nueva Orán. Nothing at Volcán is a fortification. The line is a mesh of ranches, post-houses, lookouts on high ground and mounted parties that can be raised in a night, and it works because the people who live along it are the army. Nothing Güemes personally did here is on record.
suggested_refs: The Línea del Pasaje, from Volcán in Jujuy to beyond San Ramón de la Nueva Orán

stops.name: Humahuaca, Arias takes the town
stops.date_confidence: the date is attested; the command is contradicted between sources and is not resolved here
stops.campa: On the first of March patriot forces retake Humahuaca from the royalists, capturing six cannon, five hundred rifles and prisoners. The action is led by Manuel Eduardo Arias with a hundred and fifty men. The English-language accounts credit the victory to Güemes personally; the Spanish record of De la Serna's invasion credits Arias. Both describe the same frontier command. The Guerra Gaucha is fought by subordinates acting on their own initiative across seven hundred kilometres, and the general's name absorbs what they win.
suggested_refs: The Combate de Humahuaca, 1 March 1817, under Manuel Eduardo Arias
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Invasión de De la Serna a Jujuy y Salta'
English Wikipedia, 'Martín Miguel de Güemes' (credits Güemes); contradiction flagged

stops.name: Salta, Juana Azurduy comes down from the republiquetas
stops.date_confidence: attested per juana_azurduy.journey.json; month approximate
stops.campa: Juana Azurduy, her Upper Peru republiqueta breaking apart after the death of her husband Manuel Ascencio Padilla, sends word south through the friar José Indalecio de Salazar and crosses into Salta to join Güemes. She rides with his forces for the next four years along the Salta and Jujuy quebradas. Her own journey records a tradition that the relationship went beyond commander and subordinate; contemporaries did not settle it and historians have not settled it since. Her file leaves the question open, and so does this one.
suggested_refs: Juana Azurduy's crossing into Salta, c. April 1817, via friar José Indalecio de Salazar
sources: juana_azurduy.journey.json (Salta, joining Martín Miguel de Güemes; the Salta-Jujuy frontier)

stops.name: Salta, De la Serna in the city
stops.date_confidence: attested at 15 April by the Spanish record; the English-language chronologies give 16 April without a source
stops.campa: Marshal José de la Serna's army, the largest royalist force ever sent against the north, enters Salta on the fifteenth of April. Güemes does not defend the city and does not attempt to. He blockades it: cattle driven off, mills stopped, couriers taken, every foraging party ambushed within a league of the walls. De la Serna evacuates Salta on the fifth of May and Jujuy on the twenty-first, having held both and gained nothing at all. The accounts that call this a repulse describe a battle that was never fought, because it was never offered.
suggested_refs: De la Serna's 1817 occupation of Salta and Jujuy, and the blockade that ended it
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Invasión de De la Serna a Jujuy y Salta'
English Wikipedia, 'Martín Miguel de Güemes' (gives 16 April, unsourced); contradiction flagged

stops.name: El Bañado, near El Carril, the column destroyed
stops.date_confidence: attested at 21 April 1817; an alternative dating to June 1820 circulates and is superseded, and the site coordinate is approximate
stops.campa: Six days into the occupation, gauchos destroy a royalist column at El Bañado in the country south of Salta and mortally wound Colonel Sardina. The action has been dated by one account to June 1820 and by another to April 1817, and the two datings have been treated as possibly the same fight. The record of De la Serna's invasion settles it at the twenty-first of April 1817; the June 1820 combats near Salta were fought at Chamical, Las Cañas, the Cuesta de la Pedrera and Yala. The site itself has not been fixed to a modern point.
suggested_refs: The Combate del Bañado, 21 April 1817, near El Carril
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Invasión de De la Serna a Jujuy y Salta'
Wikipedia, 'Combate del Bañado' (undated tag); contradiction noted

stops.name: Salta, the moneda de Güemes
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: A province at war for seven years, with no mint and no metal, issues its own money. Güemes authorizes the circulation of a debased silver coinage to pay for the frontier and on the twenty-sixth of October legalizes the local patriotic issue by countermark. On the twenty-fourth of May 1818 the Supreme Director in Buenos Aires annuls the feble currency outright. The province pays for the republic's war, and the republic tells the province that its money is not money.
suggested_refs: The countermarked feble coinage of Salta, 1817, annulled by Buenos Aires in May 1818

stops.name: Salta and Jujuy, two hundred and thirty-seven engagements
stops.date_confidence: the tally covers 1816-1821 and the figure is traditional, not independently verified; this date is nominal
stops.campa: Between 1816 and 1821 the frontier is invaded again and again, and tradition counts roughly two hundred and thirty-seven separate engagements of the Guerra Gaucha. The figure comes down as a tally and has never been checked against an independent list. What it describes is a war with no battles in it: hundreds of small violent nights that no dispatch summarized and no painter recorded, fought by men who went back to their herds in the morning and were carried on nobody's muster roll.
suggested_refs: The traditional tally of 237 engagements of the Guerra Gaucha
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Martín Miguel de Güemes' (traditional tally) [R]

stops.name: The Salta and Jujuy quebradas, the slow war
stops.date_confidence: nominal; the pattern runs continuously and no single date attaches to it
stops.campa: Three years of the same work: Juana Azurduy's squadron and Güemes's parties in the gorges between Salta and Jujuy, taking convoys, burning forage, letting the royalist columns walk in and then closing behind them. Nothing here is decisive and nothing here is written down at the time. The clearest description of the method is credited to the royalist general Joaquín de la Pezuela, and it was written by the man on the receiving end of it. The attribution has not been checked against an archival edition and is carried as attribution only.
stops.quote: Su plan es de no dar ni recibir batalla decisiva en parte alguna, y sí de hostilizarnos en nuestras posiciones y movimientos...experimento que nos hacen casi con impunidad una guerra lenta pero fatigosa y perjudicial.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to the royalist general Joaquín de la Pezuela on Güemes's strategy, cited in a secondary biographical compilation; primary document not located [R]
suggested_refs: The Salta-Jujuy quebradas, the working ground of the Guerra Gaucha

stops.name: San Salvador de Jujuy, the invasion of Ramírez Orozco
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: General Juan Ramírez Orozco leaves Tupiza on the eighth of May with five thousand men, occupies Jujuy on the twenty-eighth and Salta on the thirty-first, and is back in Tupiza by the fifth of July. Seven weeks, two provincial capitals taken, nothing held. De la Serna ordered the invasion but did not lead it, and the accounts that put it in February with De la Serna at its head are wrong on both counts. The combats of that June are fought at Chamical, Las Cañas, the Cuesta de la Pedrera and Yala.
suggested_refs: The 1820 royalist invasion under Juan Ramírez Orozco, Tupiza to Salta and back
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Martín Miguel de Güemes' (gives February 1820 under De la Serna, unsourced); contradiction flagged

stops.name: Salta, general in chief of the Ejército de Observación
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month not established
stops.campa: San Martín, by then on the Peruvian coast, names Güemes general in chief and puts him in command of the Ejército de Observación facing Upper Peru: the northern half of the continental plan, the hammer meant to fall on the royalist rear while San Martín works from the sea. The commission is the high point of his standing outside Salta and the beginning of his ruin inside it. To keep an army of observation he needs money, and the money comes out of a province that has been paying for this war since 1814.
suggested_refs: The Ejército de Observación sobre el Perú, commanded from Salta

stops.name: Rincón de Marlopa, Tucumán, the expedition broken
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Güemes sends roughly two thousand militiamen under Colonel Alejandro Heredia into Tucumán to depose Governor Bernabé Aráoz. At Rincón de Marlopa, two leagues south of San Miguel where the Lules meets the Manantial, Tucumán's forces under Colonel Abraham González break them. Güemes is not there; he did not ride in the campaign. Salta reads the defeat as proof that its governor is spending the province's men on quarrels between caudillos, and the merchants of the city begin to add up what he has cost them.
suggested_refs: The field of Rincón de Marlopa, also called Rincón de Ugarte, in Tucumán province
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Batalla de Rincón de Marlopa'

segments.name: The Revolución del Comercio and the Ten Days

stops.name: Salta, the Cabildo deposes him
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Revolución del Comercio breaks out on the twenty-fourth of May. The merchants, ruined by six years of forced contributions and debased coin, back the Patria Nueva faction under Evaristo de Uriburu, depose Güemes, and sign an armistice with the royalist commander Olañeta. He retakes the city briefly at the end of the month and loses it again in the first week of June. The frontier he has held for seven years is opened from behind, by his own province, in the last fortnight of his life.
suggested_refs: The Revolución del Comercio and the Patria Nueva faction of Evaristo de Uriburu

stops.name: Calle Balcarce, the Tagarete del Tineo
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The royalist partisan José María Valdés, called Barbarucho, comes down the Quebrada del Toro from Yavi on Olañeta's orders with three hundred men and enters Salta on the night of the seventh of June. Güemes is inside the city and is surrounded at the Tagarete del Tineo, the drainage ditch that is today Calle Balcarce. He is shot in the buttock and rides out through the cordon. The versions that have him shot in the back, or ambushed out in the country, are loose renderings; the Spanish record is exact about the wound and about the street.
suggested_refs: The Tagarete del Tineo, today's Calle Balcarce in Salta
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Martín Miguel de Güemes' (gives 'shot in the back', uncited); contradiction flagged

stops.name: Cañada de la Horqueta, the ten days
stops.date_confidence: attested; the exact ravine has not been fixed to a modern coordinate and this value is approximate
stops.campa: Wounded, he is carried out to a hacienda two leagues southeast of the city, in thick bush, and lies there ten days dying. The royalists offer him a surgeon and safe evacuation in exchange for ending hostilities. He refuses, and makes his officers swear to accept no arrangement of any kind that would benefit the enemy on the soil of the homeland. He dies at the Cañada de la Horqueta on the seventeenth of June, thirty-six years old. The length of the agony has bred talk of hemophilia; no male relative of the Güemes women is recorded as hemophiliac.
stops.quote: ningún tipo de trato para beneficiar al enemigo en suelo patrio
stops.quote_source: The oath Güemes demanded of his officers on his deathbed, June 1821, as reported in the Spanish Wikipedia article; a fragment embedded in article prose, not an independent document
suggested_refs: The Cañada de la Horqueta southeast of Salta, site not precisely fixed

stops.name: Capilla del Chamical, the first grave
stops.date_confidence: the burial is attested; the day is inferred from the death and the chapel site is approximate
stops.campa: His body is taken to the chapel at Chamical, southeast of Salta, and buried there. The exact site of the chapel is not established in the sources consulted and the coordinate is approximate. Several accounts move the ten days of the agony to Chamical as well; they invert the sequence, since he died at the Horqueta and was carried to the chapel afterward. The Gauchos de Güemes are dissolved with him. In 1970 the Argentine 5th Cavalry Regiment will be authorized to wear their poncho, above all on the anniversary of this week.
suggested_refs: The Capilla del Chamical, first burial place, site not precisely fixed

stops.name: Salta, retaken on the twenty-second of July
stops.date_confidence: reported by the English-language account; not independently corroborated here
stops.campa: Five weeks after his death the gauchos take Salta back for good and the royalist occupation ends. No royalist army enters the province again. The war on this frontier is over, and the men who finish it are the same ranch hands who have been fighting it since 1814, now with no general and no governor. In Buenos Aires the news of his death causes little stir. On the frontier it is answered inside five weeks, by men who hold no commission from anyone and appear in no order of battle.
suggested_refs: The final recovery of Salta, 22 July 1821

segments.name: The Afterlife of the Gaucho General

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the notice in an unnamed paper
stops.date_confidence: 1821; the exact date, the newspaper, and the wording are all uncorroborated
stops.campa: The news of the death causes no great impact in the capital. One unnamed newspaper is reported to have printed a line that has outlived every eulogy written on the other side. The paper is not named, no citation is attached, and the quotation has never been corroborated. It is set down here because it is repeated everywhere, and because indifference punctuated by contempt is the accurate description of what Buenos Aires felt about the man who had held its northern door shut for seven years.
stops.quote: Murió el abominable Güemes. Ya tenemos un cacique menos.
stops.quote_source: Unnamed Buenos Aires newspaper, 1821, quoted without citation in the Spanish Wikipedia article on Güemes [R]
suggested_refs: The uncited post-mortem notice in the Buenos Aires press, 1821

stops.name: Catedral Basílica de Salta, the Panteón de las Glorias del Norte
stops.date_confidence: the transfers are documented but their dates are not established in the sources consulted; this date is a placeholder inside the rehabilitation period
stops.campa: The bones move: from the Capilla del Chamical to the cathedral, to the Cementerio de la Santa Cruz, and at last to the Panteón de las Glorias del Norte inside the Catedral Basílica de Salta, where they lie with Antonio Álvarez de Arenales and Rudecindo Alvarado, and with Carmen Puch. The nineteenth century had filed him as a rural caudillo who stirred up the countryside. Bernardo Frías rewrote him as a disciplined commander, and Atilio Cornejo and Emilio Bidondo documented the war behind the rewriting. No forensic examination of the remains is on record.
suggested_refs: The Panteón de las Glorias del Norte inside the Catedral Basílica de Salta
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Panteón de las Glorias del Norte'

stops.name: Cerro San Bernardo, the monument
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: At the foot of the Cerro San Bernardo, on the spot where the wounded man first fell from his horse while riding out toward the Horqueta, the nation raises twenty-five metres of stone quarried from the hill itself, blocks of more than seventy-five kilograms each, with bronzes assembled by the artisans of the Arsenal Esteban de Luca. Víctor Juan Garino sculpts it, Andrés Iñigo directs the architecture, and it is inaugurated on the twentieth of February 1931 with President José Félix Uriburu present. Eleven years of work to mark where a man came off a horse.
suggested_refs: The Monumento a Güemes, Av. Uruguay 4400, Salta, built 1920-1931

stops.name: Salta and the Republic, the seventeenth of June
stops.date_confidence: the laws run 1999 to 2016; this date marks the first nationwide observance
stops.campa: Law 25.172 makes the seventeenth of June the National Day of Latin American Liberty; Law 26.125 declares Güemes a National Hero; Law 27.258 makes the day a national holiday, kept in Salta from 2014 and across the country from 2016. Tarija in Bolivia is said to have adopted the date by decree in 2019, though the claim carries a citation-needed tag and names a national instrument for what would be a departmental act. In 2022 a Cretaceous abelisaurid dug out of Salta province is named Guemesia ochoai.
suggested_refs: Argentine Laws 25.172, 26.125 and 27.258; the abelisaurid Guemesia ochoai (2022)
